steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper presenting the first modular robots shaped as rhombic dodecahedra. Start from the history of the shape, cover where it occurs in nature, review unit shapes used in modular robotics, and explain why rhombic dodecahedra could beat cubes.

steps.name: skeleton_outline

- The shape in natural crystals and why it matters for self-assembly
- Space-filling modular robots

- Parallelohedra: cube and rhombic dodecahedron are simplest
- Kinematic advantage of rhombic dodecahedra over cubes
- Our contribution: first rhombic dodecahedra robots

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
When Johannes Kepler looked into the hexagonal cells of honeycombs he saw three rhombi at their base. By capping a cell with three more rhombi, Kepler sketched a rhombic dodecahedron. But the shape was already on his mind. When studying how snowflakes could be built out of microscopic spheres of ice, Kepler made the following conjecture: no packing of congruent spheres has a density greater than the face-centered cubic packing, in which each sphere touches 12 others and which fills just over 74% of space. If these spheres are uniformly compressed, they deform into space-filling polyhedra with twelve faces, which are rhombic dodecahedra.

Since Kepler discovered the shape in the early 17th century, rhombic dodecahedra have been found in crystals of viruses, proteins, carbohydrates, metals and minerals. These self-assembling crystalline structures have been of interest in several fields of engineering because of their exceptional optical, catalytic, electronic and magnetic properties, and this suggests that space filling in general, and the dodecahedral morphology in particular, could also be useful for self-assembling modular robots.

Modular robots are like crystals in that they can "grow" multicellular bodies by combining and separating unit cells. If such robots were space-filling, they could form gapless containers, pipes, mirrors, shields, submersibles, spaceships and extraterrestrial habitats on the fly. And because they have broader surface contacts between neighbors, space-filling robots could build superstructures that are much more stable and energetically favorable than robots that are not space-filling.

- Unit shapes explored
  - triangles, hexagons, spheres, cubes, cuboids, cylinders, semi-cylinders, cylindroids (cite each)
  - only spheres and cubes attach in 3D; only cubes fill space
- Parallelohedra
  - cube is a parallelohedron (cite): congruent polyhedron filling space by translation only, regular lattice
  - four others: rhombic dodecahedron, hexagonal prism, elongated dodecahedron, truncated octahedron (face types)
  - cube + rhombic dodecahedron simplest; isometric faces -> connect on all sides, simpler assembly/reconfiguration
  - infinitude of other space-filling polyhedra/tilings; only cube taken seriously; most modular robots cubes or cuboids (cite)
- Kinematics
  - first noted by earlier work (cite)
  - cubes: two difficult rotations (90, 180 degrees), sliding friction against perpendicular cubes
  - rhombic dodecahedra: single 120 degree rotation, no sliding; keep cube's property of aligned faces after rotation about one of four shared edges
- Contribution
  - earlier work (cite) coordinated self-assembly of virtual rhombic dodecahedra toward target shapes; no such robots built

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
When Johannes Kepler looked into the hexagonal cells of honeycombs he saw three rhombi at their base. By capping a cell with three more rhombi, Kepler sketched a rhombic dodecahedron. But the shape was already on his mind. When studying how snowflakes could be built out of microscopic spheres of ice, Kepler made the following conjecture: no packing of congruent spheres has a density greater than the face-centered cubic packing, in which each sphere touches 12 others and which fills just over 74% of space. If these spheres are uniformly compressed, they deform into space-filling polyhedra with twelve faces, which are rhombic dodecahedra.

Since Kepler discovered the shape in the early 17th century, rhombic dodecahedra have been found in crystals of viruses, proteins, carbohydrates, metals and minerals. These self-assembling crystalline structures have been of interest in several fields of engineering because of their exceptional optical, catalytic, electronic and magnetic properties, and this suggests that space filling in general, and the dodecahedral morphology in particular, could also be useful for self-assembling modular robots.

Modular robots are like crystals in that they can "grow" multicellular bodies by combining and separating unit cells. If such robots were space-filling, they could form gapless containers, pipes, mirrors, shields, submersibles, spaceships and extraterrestrial habitats on the fly. And because they have broader surface contacts between neighbors, space-filling robots could build superstructures that are much more stable and energetically favorable than robots that are not space-filling.

Lots of unit shapes have been explored in robotics: triangles, hexagons, spheres, cubes, cuboids, cylinders, semi-cylinders and cylindroids. But only two of these shapes were built to attach in 3D space, spheres and cubes, and only cubes were able to fill it.

The cube is a parallelohedron, which is a congruent polyhedron that can be translated to fill space completely, without rotations. So space can be partitioned into a regular lattice by cubes. Besides the cube, which has square faces, there are only four other parallelohedra: the rhombic dodecahedron (rhombic faces), the hexagonal prism (hexagonal and cubic faces), the elongated dodecahedron (rhombic and octagonal faces), and the truncated octahedron (cubic, rhombic, and hexagonal faces). The cube and the rhombic dodecahedron are the simplest parallelohedra. Their faces are isometric (all squares or all rhombi), which lets two cells connect on all sides, and this makes assembling and reconfiguring multicellular bodies simpler.

There are infinitely many other polyhedra that can fill space without gaps, alone or combined with other polyhedra, through translations, rotations or reflections, along periodic or aperiodic tilings. Of all these shapes only the cube has been taken seriously in robotics. In fact most modular robots built so far have been cubes or cuboids.

Rhombic dodecahedra have a kinematic advantage over cubes that was first noted by earlier work: Cubes need two kinds of rolling/rotational motions that are inherently difficult (90 \degree and 180 \degree; Fig. 2 A and B) to move around each other, and they can have considerable sliding friction against any cubes that are perpendicular to the axis of rotation. Rhombic dodecahedra on the other hand need only one simple rotational movement (120°; Fig. 2 C), and there is no need for any part of the cells to slide against each other, while they keep the good property of cubes: once two opposing faces of two cells are aligned and connected, every rotation about one of the four shared edges will give another pair of aligned faces.

After illustrating this, the same work went on to show how to coordinate the self-assembly of virtual rhombic dodecahedra toward target shapes, but until now nobody has created such robots. So here we design and deploy the first rhombic dodecahedra robots. They cannot assemble themselves yet, but their physicality helps us envisage a future in which they do.

steps.text:
When Johannes Kepler peered into the hexagonal cells of honeycombs he saw three rhombi at their base (Fig. A non-cubic space-filling modular robot A,B). Capping a cell with three more rhombi, Kepler sketched a rhombic dodecahedron. But the shape was already on his mind. Studying how snowflakes could be built from microscopic spheres of ice, Kepler made the following conjecture [1]: no packing of congruent spheres has density greater than that of the face-centered cubic packing (Fig. A non-cubic space-filling modular robot C), in which each sphere touches 12 others and which fills just over 74% of space. When uniformly compressed, these spheres deform into space-filling polyhedra with twelve faces: rhombic dodecahedra (Fig. A non-cubic space-filling modular robot D).

Since Kepler's discovery of the shape in the early 17th century, rhombic dodecahedra have been found in crystals of viruses [3], proteins [4], carbohydrates [5], metals [6] and minerals [7]. These self-assembling crystalline structures have been of keen interest in several fields of engineering due to their exceptional optical, catalytic, electronic and magnetic properties [8,9], which suggests that space filling in general, and the dodecahedral morphology in particular, may also be useful for self-assembling modular robots [10].

Like crystals, modular robots can "grow" to form multicellular bodies by combining and separating unit cells. Such robots, if space-filling, could form gapless containers, pipes, mirrors, shields, submersibles, spaceships and extraterrestrial habitats on the fly. And by virtue of broader surface contacts between neighbors, space-filling robots could build much more stable and energetically favorable superstructures than non-space-filling robots [11].

Many unit shapes have been explored in robotics: triangles [12], hexagons [13], spheres [14], cubes [15], cuboids [16], cylinders [17], semi-cylinders [18] and cylindroids [19]. But only two of these shapes (spheres and cubes) were built to attach in 3D space, and only one was capable of filling it: cubes.

The cube is a parallelohedron [20]: a congruent polyhedron that can be translated to completely fill space, without rotations. In other words, cubes can partition space into a regular lattice. In addition to the cube, which has square faces, there are just four other parallelohedra: the rhombic dodecahedron (rhombic faces), the hexagonal prism (hexagonal and cubic faces), the elongated dodecahedron (rhombic and octagonal faces), and the truncated octahedron (cubic, rhombic, and hexagonal faces). The cube and the rhombic dodecahedron are the simplest parallelohedra. Their isometric faces (all squares or all rhombi) allow two cells to connect on all sides, which simplifies the assembly and reconfiguration of multicellular bodies.

There is an infinitude of other polyhedra that, alone or in combination with additional polyhedra, via translations, rotations or reflections, along periodic or aperiodic tilings, can fill space without gaps. Out of all these possible shapes, only the cube has been taken seriously in robotics. Indeed, the vast majority of modular robots built to date have been cubes or cuboids [21].

Rhombic dodecahedra have a kinematic advantage over cubes that was first noted by [22]: Cubes require two kinds of inherently difficult rolling/rotational motions (90 \degree and 180 \degree; Fig. 2 A and B) to move about each other, and can incur considerable sliding friction against any cubes perpendicular to the axis of rotation. Rhombic dodecahedra, in contrast, require only a single simple rotational movement (120°; Fig. 2 C) and eliminate the need for any part of the cells to slide against each other, while preserving the good property of cubes: once two opposing faces of two cells are aligned and connected, all rotations about one of the four shared edges result in another pair of aligned faces.

After illustrating this, [22] went on to show how to coordinate the self-assembly of virtual rhombic dodecahedra toward target shapes, but until now no such robots have been created. Thus, here we design and deploy the first rhombic dodecahedra robots. While they cannot yet assemble themselves, their physicality helps us envisage a future in which they do.
